questions.prompt: A city report fits monthly consumption on tariff band, household size and temperature for all billed households and writes: "The social tariff makes families use 9% less water." Which sentence does the analysis support?
options: Households on the social tariff used about 9% less water than comparable households on other tariffs in the data
Moving a family to the social tariff would cut its use by about 9%
The social tariff caused a 9% saving once size and temperature were controlled
Nothing, because regression on observational data supports no statement
questions.explanation: The data compare different households, so they support a description of the difference between groups, not a claim about what the tariff does.
misconceptions: Reads a comparison between groups of households as the effect of changing one household's tariff
Believes that adjusting for some variables turns a comparison into a causal estimate
Treats descriptive use as worthless: a stated comparison in a stated population is a valid result

questions.prompt: Ghaliya asks: "How much more water does a household with one more person use, in our villa districts?" Which is the estimand?
options: The coefficient of household size in a model of log consumption
The R squared of a model that includes household size
The average difference in monthly cubic metres between villa households and the same households with one more person
The p-value of household size in a model fitted to all bands
questions.explanation: An estimand names the population, the outcome with its unit and the comparison; a coefficient, a fit statistic or a p-value is a property of a model, not the quantity asked about.
misconceptions: Confuses a model's coefficient, on its own scale, with the quantity the question asks for
Takes a measure of fit for an answer to a question about size
Takes a test statistic for the quantity of interest and ignores the population named

questions.prompt: You simulate 200 data sets from a known model, fit each, and find that 81% of the 95% intervals for one coefficient contain its planted value. What does that tell you?
options: The planted value is probably wrong
The intervals are too narrow for this design, so the standard errors or the model are wrong for it
The estimates are biased, so the model should be refitted on real data
Nothing: 81% is within the normal noise of 200 repeats
questions.explanation: With 200 repeats, coverage of a correct 95% interval falls between about 92% and 98%; 81% means the intervals understate the uncertainty.
misconceptions: Forgets that in fake data the planted value is known exactly
Confuses under-coverage with bias: intervals can miss because they are too narrow around unbiased estimates
Overestimates the simulation noise of a coverage count over 200 repeats

questions.prompt: A model that recovers every planted coefficient from fake data has been shown to describe the real bills well.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Recovering a planted model checks the code and the estimator; whether the real data follow the model is checked against the data.
misconceptions: Confuses a test of the method with a test of the model against the world

questions.prompt: A model of log monthly consumption has a residual standard deviation of 0.30. For one household type it predicts 3.00 on the log scale. What is the best estimate of that type's mean consumption?
options: exp(3.00), about 20.1 cubic metres
exp(3.30), about 27.1 cubic metres
3.00 cubic metres
exp(3.045), about 21.0 cubic metres
questions.explanation: With normal errors on the log scale the mean is exp(prediction + sigma squared / 2) = exp(3.00 + 0.045).
misconceptions: Takes the median, exp(prediction), for the mean
Adds sigma instead of sigma squared over two
Forgets to back-transform from the log scale

questions.prompt: A spline fit on 40,000 bills gives a 95% band of 37.3 to 38.4 cubic metres at 40 °C for four-person standard households. A customer of that type disputes a bill of 46 cubic metres. What does the band say about the bill?
options: Nothing direct: the band is for the mean of such households, and single bills spread far wider
The bill is almost certainly a meter error, since it lies outside the band
The bill should be cut to 38.4 cubic metres
The model is wrong, since a real bill falls outside its band
questions.explanation: An interval for the mean narrows as data grow; an interval for one household includes the household-to-household spread and is many times wider.
misconceptions: Reads an interval for the mean as the range of single bills
Uses the mean band as a ceiling for an individual bill
Expects individual observations to fall inside an interval for the mean

questions.prompt: In log_m3 ~ tariff_band * household_size, the household_size coefficient is 0.096 and tariff_band[T.social]:household_size is -0.022. What is the social band's slope for household size on the log scale?
questions.explanation: The reference band's slope plus the social interaction term: 0.096 - 0.022 = 0.074, about 7.7% per person.
misconceptions: Reads the interaction term as the band's slope; it is a difference between slopes
Ignores the interaction and applies the reference band's slope
Adds the size of the interaction instead of its signed value

questions.prompt: On the log scale, one more person goes with 7.6% more consumption on the social band and 12.1% more on the villa band. In cubic metres a month, the villa effect turns out more than three times the social one. Why?
options: The percentages were computed wrongly
The interval for villas is wider
Villas have fewer households in the data
The same percentage applies to a higher base: villas use far more water to begin with
questions.explanation: An effect in cubic metres is the percentage times each household's level, so a larger base turns similar percentages into much larger volumes.
misconceptions: Assumes the two scales must agree in ratio
Confuses the width of an interval with the size of an effect
Confuses the number of rows with the size of an effect

questions.prompt: For each district and month, a utility records the number of meter faults and the number of meters installed. Which model fits the question "how does the fault rate differ by meter age?"
options: A linear model of the number of faults
A logistic model of whether the district had any fault
A Poisson or negative binomial model of faults with log meters as an offset
A linear model of faults divided by meters, without weights
questions.explanation: The outcome is a count with an exposure (meters), so a count model with log exposure as an offset describes the rate per meter.
misconceptions: Treats a count as a continuous outcome, which allows negative predictions and ignores exposure
Throws away the counts by reducing them to a flag
Divides by exposure but treats a rate from 10 meters as exactly as reliable as one from 10,000

questions.prompt: A linear probability model can predict a negative probability for some households even when it fits the average difference well.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A line subtracts the same amount from every row, so rows that start near zero are pushed below it; the average difference can still be right.
misconceptions: Believes that a model which gets the average right must get every prediction into range

questions.prompt: In a logistic model of late payment, the odds ratio for each past late payment is 1.6. A household has a 20% probability of a late bill. About what is the probability for the same household with one more past late payment?
questions.explanation: Odds 0.2/0.8 = 0.25; times 1.6 is 0.40; a probability of 0.40/1.40, about 29%.
misconceptions: Multiplies the probability by the odds ratio
Adds the odds ratio's excess as percentage points
Adds 16 points as if the odds ratio were a difference on the probability scale

questions.prompt: Bills on autopay were late 40 points less often than comparable bills without it, in a logistic model of observational data. Which sentence may go in the collections report?
options: Comparable households on autopay paid late about 40 points less often than those without it
Enrolling households in autopay will cut their late payment by 40 points
Autopay reduces late payment by 90%, as its odds ratio is 0.1
Autopay causes on-time payment for most households
questions.explanation: Households chose autopay, so the data support a comparison of households, not a statement of what enrolling them would do.
misconceptions: Reads a comparison of self-selected groups as the effect of an action
Reads an odds ratio as a cut in probability and adds a causal claim
Turns an association into a causal claim about most households

questions.prompt: In a Poisson model of leaks with offset log(kilometre-years), the coefficient of pressure is 0.28. What does exp(0.28) = 1.32 mean?
options: Each extra bar goes with 1.32 more leaks a year on every main
Each extra bar goes with 32% more leaks per kilometre-year, other terms equal
Each extra bar adds 0.28 leaks per kilometre
A main at high pressure is 1.32 kilometres longer on average
questions.explanation: With a log link and an exposure offset, exp(coefficient) is a rate ratio per kilometre-year.
misconceptions: Reads a rate ratio as a difference in counts
Reads the log-scale coefficient as a difference in rate
Confuses the offset with an outcome

questions.prompt: A Poisson model of complaints per district-month has a Pearson dispersion of 4.0. A colleague reports a rate ratio for pressure management of 1.40 with a 95% interval of 1.20 to 1.63. What do you tell them?
options: The interval is about right, since dispersion affects only the fit
The estimate is biased upward by a factor of 4
Use a linear model instead, because counts with dispersion are not Poisson
The interval is too narrow; refit with a negative binomial or scale the errors, which roughly doubles its width on the log scale
questions.explanation: With dispersion 4, standard errors are too small by about the square root of 4, so the log-scale interval should be about twice as wide.
misconceptions: Believes overdispersion leaves the uncertainty unchanged
Thinks overdispersion biases the rate ratio by the dispersion factor
Abandons the count family instead of widening the variance
